newsitem.title: UK: Survey sees 1.6 mln new jobs in UK in 10 years.
newsitem.headline: Survey sees 1.6 mln new jobs in UK in 10 years.

text.p: Around 1.6 million extra jobs will be created in Britain over the next 10 years, half of which will be part-time and half of which will be in self-employment, according to a study by Business Strategies Ltd.
The business and economic forecasting consultancy said virtually no extra full-time jobs would be created and unemployment would remain relatively high at around two million.
"With employers creating almost no extra full-time jobs, 790,000 more people will opt for self-employment between now and 2006," the study said.
There would be another 770,000 extra jobs for employees by 2006 but almost all would be part-time, with many in personal services such as child care and catering.
"Women will capture two-thirds of the total growth in work," Business Strategies said. It expects around 1.5 million men to work part-time for employers in 2006 compared with 1.3 million this year.

"The extra jobs will do little to bring down the number of people registered as unemployed, which we forecast will fall by just 131,000 between 1996 and 2006 to a figure of 1.99 million," said Business Strategies director Richard Holt.
Seasonally adjusted unemployment was 2.073 million in September.

Holt said skills and qualifications were the key to success in the job market but some skills would be far more useful than others. "For those pursuing the self-employment route, management skills will matter as well as vocational ones."

The study, entitled "Occupations in the Future," assumes GDP growth will average 2.4 percent a year until 2002. It estimates the workforce at 26.976 million people in 2006 compared with 25.423 million this year.
- the largest increase in self-employment will be for highly skilled workers, ranging from designers to computer programmers;
- the sector with the fastest predicted employment growth in the next 10 years is financial and business services;
- there will be many more self-employed professionals and sole proprietors as well as traditional skilled construction workers;
- the fastest rise in employment overall will be for professionals such as lawyers, accountants and doctors;
- farm labourers are set to see the fastest decline in overall jobs (down 14 percent), closely followed by skilled engineering workers (down 13 percent;
- the number of managers and administrators is likely to increase by around 400,000 to 4.6 million.
